title: Exit Strategy: Hold, Refinance, Sell, or 1031 Exchange

slides.kicker: Phase 2 · Operations launch · Final lesson of the track
slides.title: Every exit spends the same equity, so price all four options before you pick one
slides.subtitle: Lesson OP.12. Exit Strategy: Hold, Refinance, Sell, or 1031 Exchange
meta: Education only. Not tax, legal, or lending advice. Tax rates shown are placeholders.
slides.notes:
This is the last lesson in the STR Concierge track, and it's about the end of an investment, or at least a turning point.

You have four options for a property you own. You can hold it, refinance it, sell it, or sell it through a 1031 exchange. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to put those four side by side. You'll compare them on after-tax proceeds, future debt, time, and workload.

You'll also learn how the gain on a sale is built, which parts depreciation touches, and which answers only your CPA can give. I'm not going to calculate your tax. I'm going to show you the structure so you can collect the right records and read your CPA's answer.

You'll leave with a decision worksheet you can hand to that CPA and to a qualified intermediary. We'll use Cedar Ridge at the end of year 5.

slides.title: Each option answers one question: is this equity doing more here than elsewhere?
rows: Some of it comes out as a new, bigger loan
It turns into cash, minus taxes
It moves into another investment property, and the tax may be deferred

box.label: Weigh five things
box.text: After-tax cash, time to complete, future debt, the work you keep doing, and what you give up (opportunity cost). No option wins on all five.

slides.notes:
Every exit decision comes down to one question. Is the equity in this property doing more for you here than it would do somewhere else?

Equity is the value you could turn into cash. That's market value minus the loan balance, minus the costs of getting it out. Holding keeps that equity in the house. Refinancing pulls some of it out as a new loan. Selling turns it into cash, minus taxes. And a 1031 exchange moves it into another investment property and may defer the tax.

Each option mixes five things differently: after-tax cash, time, future debt, ongoing work, and opportunity cost. None of them wins on all five. You're choosing a trade-off you can live with.

You'll make this call more than once. Run it whenever your review from Sam's OP.10 shows a real change. A big capital repair, a new local rule, a life change, or equity that has outgrown the cash flow.

slides.title: Start with an honest equity number built from four documented inputs
slides.keyline: Value - loan balance - selling costs = net proceeds before income tax
items: Updated value: a broker's opinion, recent comparable sales, or an appraisal. Not the price you'd like.
Ask the broker whether buyers in your market pay extra for furniture and future bookings.
Loan balance: the servicer's latest statement. If you plan to sell, request a payoff quote.
Capital repairs due soon, like a roof, HVAC, or deck. They change the hold case and the sale price.
Selling costs: commissions, transfer taxes, title and closing fees, concessions. Get your agent's net sheet.
slides.notes:
Four inputs start every exit analysis.

The first is the updated value. Get it from a broker's opinion of value, recent comparable sales, or an appraisal. Don't use the price you'd like. Short-term rental houses sometimes sell with furniture and bookings, so ask the broker whether buyers in your market actually pay for that.

The second is the loan balance. Take it from the servicer's latest statement, not your own amortization schedule. If you plan to sell, request a payoff quote. It can include items the statement doesn't show.

The third is capital repairs coming in the next few years. A roof or HVAC replacement changes the hold case. It can also change the sale price if a buyer's inspector finds it.

The fourth is the cost of selling. Our example uses 7% of value as an assumption. Your agent can give you a line-by-line net sheet.

The result is net proceeds before income tax. That's not your spendable number yet.

slides.title: Holding has a cost you never see on a statement: what the equity could earn elsewhere
rows: It covers costs in a weak season, repairs are funded, the work is manageable, or a sale would trigger tax you'd rather defer
You have a specific, better use for the cash and the property can carry the bigger loan in a weak year
More debt and payments; no sale, so no tax on a gain
The property no longer fits your goals, local rules tightened, a big repair won't pay back, or the equity has a clearly better use

box.label: Opportunity cost in one line
box.text: A property earning $5,000 a year on $140,000 of equity earns about 3.6%. If safer money pays similar, holding carries more risk for the same return.

slides.notes:
Holding is the default. It needs no transaction. But it has a cost you don't see on any statement.

Say a property earns $5,000 a year on $140,000 of equity. Both numbers are assumptions. That equity is earning about 3.6%. If you could sell and put the after-tax cash somewhere safer at a similar return, holding carries more risk for the same money. That's opportunity cost.

Holding makes sense when the property still covers its costs in a weak season, the capital repairs are funded, and the work is manageable. It also makes sense when a sale would trigger a big tax bill you'd rather defer, and the property still meets your PA.1 goals.

Refinancing keeps the property and pulls out cash. It doesn't trigger tax on a gain, but it adds debt. Refinance when you have a specific use for the cash.

Selling ends the risk and the work. It also brings the tax consequences we'll look at next.

slides.title: Gain is what you realize minus adjusted basis, and depreciation shrinks the basis

nodes.d: Roughly the sale price minus selling costs
What you paid plus certain acquisition costs, plus improvements, minus depreciation
Into pieces that can be taxed differently

box.label: Allowed or allowable
box.text: Depreciation reduces basis whether or not you claimed it (Pub 527). Skipping it only loses the deduction. Bonus depreciation and section 179 also reduce basis.

slides.notes:
You don't need to calculate your own tax. You do need to know how the calculation is built, so you can collect the right records and read your CPA's answer. Every rule here depends on your facts and the tax year.

Gain equals amount realized minus adjusted basis. Amount realized is roughly the sale price minus selling costs. Adjusted basis starts with what you paid plus certain acquisition costs. It goes up by improvements and down by depreciation. IRS Publication 544 describes it that way.

Now the part that surprises people. Suppose you didn't claim all the depreciation you were entitled to. Publication 527 says you still reduce basis by the full amount you could have deducted. The IRS phrase is allowed or allowable. So skipping depreciation doesn't protect you at sale. It only means you lost the deduction.

Publication 527 also says bonus depreciation and any section 179 deduction reduce basis.

slides.title: Your CPA splits the gain into three pieces, and cost segregation grows the ordinary one
rows: Furniture and building parts a study moved to 5- or 7-year lives
Ordinary income, up to the lesser of that depreciation or the gain on those assets (Pub 544)
Gain tied to straight-line depreciation on the building
Netted by your CPA with your other gains and losses (Pub 544)
slides.caption: 15-year land improvements can be treated differently; your CPA classifies each asset. Also ask about suspended passive losses (Pub 925) and state tax. Neither is modeled here.

box.label: Cost segregation at sale
box.text: Faster deductions shrink basis faster, so more of the gain can land in the ordinary bucket. The study mostly changes timing. SR.3 is the tool for that talk.

slides.notes:
Your CPA splits the gain. Here's the structure.

First, personal property. That includes furniture and many building parts a cost-segregation study moves to 5- or 7-year lives. It's generally section 1245 property. Publication 544 says gain on it is ordinary income to the extent of depreciation allowed or allowable. The ordinary part is the lesser of that depreciation or the gain on those assets. So it depends on how much of the price gets allocated to those items. That's a CPA and appraisal question.

Second, the building itself is section 1250 property. Gain tied to straight-line depreciation on it is taxed at a maximum 25% rate, per IRS Topic 409.

Third, anything left is section 1231 gain.

This is where Sam's PA.5 lesson comes back. A study moves deductions earlier. At sale, more of the gain can land in the ordinary bucket. It can still be worth doing. Resource SR.3 is how you have that conversation.

slides.title: A 1031 exchange covers real property held for business or investment, not the furniture
items: Since 2018, only real property held for use in a business or for investment. That applies to both properties.
Real property held primarily for sale doesn't qualify.
Property used mainly for personal use doesn't qualify: a primary residence, second home, or vacation home.
Furniture, equipment, and other personal property generally no longer qualify after 2017.
The gain is deferred, not erased. Ask your CPA how it affects the new property's basis and depreciation.

box.label: If you stay there too
box.text: Rev. Proc. 2008-16 is a safe harbor for units with occasional personal use. Have your CPA confirm its section 4.02 standards against the IRS text.

slides.notes:
A like-kind exchange under section 1031 lets you sell one investment property and buy another. You defer the gain instead of paying tax on it now. Deferred means it waits. Ask your CPA how the deferred gain affects the replacement property's basis and future depreciation.

What qualifies? Since 2018, only real property held for use in a business or for investment. Both the property you sell and the one you buy have to be held that way. The IRS says property used primarily for personal use, like a primary residence, second home, or vacation home, doesn't qualify. And personal property generally no longer qualifies. So the furniture in your STR generally can't be part of the exchange.

Now the caveat for owners who also stay at the property. The IRS issued Rev. Proc. 2008-16, a safe harbor for a unit with occasional personal use. Summaries describe holding, rental, and personal-use conditions. Have your CPA confirm those specifics against the IRS text before you rely on them.

slides.title: Five gates decide whether an exchange can work before you list the property

gates.q: Is the property held for business or investment use?
gates.sub: Both the one you sell and the one you buy.

gates.q: Does your personal use fit Rev. Proc. 2008-16, or do your facts support investment use?
Is your qualified intermediary independent of you?
gates.sub: Not your agent, broker, accountant, attorney, or employee, now or in the past 2 years.

gates.q: Can you identify replacements in writing, signed, by day 45?
Can you receive the replacement by day 180 or your return due date, whichever is earlier?

slides.end: All five pass: the gain on the real property may be deferred. Report it on Form 8824.
slides.notes:
Here's the exchange as a set of gates. Any No stops it or sends you to your CPA.

Gate one: both properties held for business or investment. Gate two: your personal use either fits Rev. Proc. 2008-16 or your facts otherwise support investment use. Outside the safe harbor it depends on your facts, so don't assume.

Gate three is the qualified intermediary, the QI. In a deferred exchange the QI holds the sale proceeds. Your own agent can't serve. The IRS list includes your real estate agent or broker, accountant, attorney, and employee, and anyone in those roles in the past two years. The IRS also warns that some intermediaries have gone bankrupt or failed to perform. Ask how funds are held, what bonding or insurance exists, and who signs withdrawals.

Gates four and five are the clock. Identify in writing by day 45. Receive the replacement by day 180 or your return due date, whichever comes first. The IRS treats both as strict.

slides.title: At year 5, Cedar Ridge holds $142,560 of equity before any income tax
slides.side:
They paid down $16,231 of principal in five years.

**Hold:** base cash flow of $5,572 is **3.9%** on that equity. The weak case is -$5,475 (B4). Appreciation isn't spendable income.
slides.notes:
Here's Cedar Ridge at the end of year 5. Maya and Chris kept the original DSCR loan and never refinanced. This is our canonical case B8. Every figure is an assumption, and the tax rates you'll see are placeholders for a CPA to replace.

Value is $446,321, from 3% a year growth. The loan balance is $272,519, so they've paid down $16,231 of principal. Selling costs at 7% are $31,242. That leaves $142,560 of net proceeds before income tax.

Now the hold case. Our model keeps NOI flat, so base-case cash flow is still $5,572, and the weak case is still minus $5,475. On $142,560 of equity, the base case earns 3.9%.

One note on those figures. They use the original underwriting, B1. PA.9's diligence added $400 a year, the permit renewal. Take $400 off every cash flow in this example. The hold becomes $5,172 and minus $5,875, which is 3.6% on the equity. The year-5 refinance becomes $2,085 and minus $8,962. The ranking of the options doesn't change.

That's before appreciation. Appreciation is real, but you can't spend it unless you sell or borrow against it. So compare the 3.9% against what that equity could do elsewhere.

slides.title: A year-5 refinance pulls out $53,853 but shrinks base cash flow to $2,485
slides.side:
New principal and interest at 7.0%: **$26,724 a year**.

Cash flow after: base **$2,485**, weak **-$8,562**.
slides.notes:
Now suppose they refinance at year 5 instead, using the same B7 terms. That's 75% loan-to-value, 2.5% costs, and a 7.0% rate. All assumptions.

The new loan is $334,741. Pay off the $272,519 balance and the $8,369 of costs, and they walk away with $53,853 in cash. They keep the property.

But look at the other side. The new principal and interest is $26,724 a year. Base-case cash flow drops to $2,485. And a weak year now costs them $8,562 instead of $5,475.

So the refinance trades a thinner margin for cash now. It doesn't trigger tax on a gain, because nothing was sold. Whether that's a good trade depends on what the $53,853 is for. If they don't have a specific, better use for it, they've just taken on more debt.

slides.title: A cost-segregation study nearly doubles the gain at sale, from $64,184 to $124,175
slides.caption: Simplified: full-year straight-line for five years; building at 39 years ($8,021 or $6,256 a year). Real figures depend on placed-in-service dates and conventions.
slides.notes:
Now the sale, built two ways. The amount realized is the same in both: $446,321 minus $31,242 of selling costs, or $415,079. What changes is the adjusted basis, and that depends on how they depreciated.

I simplified here. Full-year straight-line for five years, with the building on 39 years.

In Scenario A there's no cost-segregation study. They took bonus on the $32,000 of furniture and $8,021 a year on the building. Total depreciation is $72,105, so adjusted basis is $350,895 and the gain is $64,184.

In Scenario B they used the B6 study with 100% bonus. The reclassified building parts, $68,816, came off in year one, plus the furniture. The remaining building ran at $6,256 a year. Total depreciation is $132,096. Adjusted basis drops to $290,904, and the gain is $124,175.

Same house, same sale price. The depreciation choice nearly doubles the gain.

slides.title: The study moved deductions forward, and it didn't erase the tax
slides.caption: Allocations assumed: $6,000 to used furniture in both; plus $30,000 to reclassified parts in B, all treated as section 1245 for simplicity.

box.label: Check the logic
box.text: B took $59,991 more depreciation. At 32% that's up to $19,197 of earlier savings, if the losses were usable. At sale, B pays $13,216 more tax.

slides.notes:
Now the split. The recapture depends on how much of the price is allocated to section 1245 items. I assumed $6,000 for the used furniture in both scenarios, plus $30,000 for the reclassified building parts in Scenario B. Those allocations are assumptions only.

The rates are placeholders too: 32% on the ordinary piece, 25% on the section 1250 piece because that's the maximum in Topic 409, and 15% on the rest. Illustrative federal tax is $14,658 in A and $27,874 in B.

Check the logic. Scenario B took $59,991 more depreciation over five years. At 32% that's up to $19,197 of earlier tax savings, but only if the losses were usable when they were taken. At sale, B pays $13,216 more.

After tax, they'd walk away with $127,902 in A or $114,686 in B. And holding earns 4.4% or 4.9% on those after-tax figures. The equity you'd actually leave with is smaller than the equity on paper.

slides.title: An October 20, 2031 sale sets a December 4 identification deadline

nodes.d: Sale closes. The QI holds the proceeds.
Written, signed identification of possible replacements
Receive the replacement, unless the 2031 return due date comes first
Confirms the deadline, any extension, and Form 8824

box.label: Inside those 180 days
box.text: Permission check (SR.1), underwriting (Sam's PA.4), financing (PA.6, PA.7), and a team (OP.7). Have the shortlist ready before the sale closes.

slides.notes:
Now the 1031 path. Suppose they sell on October 20, 2031, and want to exchange. The dates are assumptions.

Day 45 is December 4, 2031. That's the written identification deadline. Day 180 is April 17, 2032. That can be later than the due date of their 2031 return. If it is, the return due date comes first unless they extend. Their CPA confirms the exact date.

If the exchange qualifies, the gain on the real property is deferred. The furniture sits outside the exchange, so the CPA handles that $6,000 allocation separately. Their 10 personal-use days a year are the Rev. Proc. 2008-16 question. They need calendar records for the two years before the sale, and a plan for the two years after.

The exchange also restarts the whole buying process. The replacement needs its own address check, underwriting, financing, and team, all inside 180 days. That clock argues for having the replacement shortlist ready before the sale closes.

slides.title: Side by side, the numbers show the trade-offs but don't pick for Maya and Chris
rows: Bigger loan in a weak year
slides.caption: Sell figures are after illustrative federal tax. Which is right depends on their PA.1 goals and their worksheet answers.
slides.notes:
Here's how the four options line up for Maya and Chris.

Hold gives them no cash now, keeps $272,519 of debt, and keeps the $5,572 base and minus $5,475 weak case. The work stays the same. The risk is weak seasons and capital repairs.

Refinance gives them $53,853 now, with $334,741 of debt. Base cash flow drops to $2,485 and a weak year costs $8,562. Same work, bigger loan.

Sell gives them $127,902 or $114,686 after illustrative tax, depending on how they depreciated. No debt, no work. The risk moves to paying the tax and finding a use for the cash.

The exchange reinvests everything into a new property with a new loan. The work restarts, and the risks are the deadlines, the QI, and qualification.

Which one is right depends on their goals from PA.1 and their answers in the worksheet. The numbers make the trade-offs visible. They don't pick for you.

[Recording note: Preston can add a real example here if he has one.]

slides.title: Fill one column per option, and date every figure you enter
slides.text: Part B of the exit worksheet. Attach your trailing-12 from OP.11 and your Part A starting facts.
rows: Hours a month of your time afterward
slides.notes:
Now your worksheet. It has three parts.

Part A is your starting facts. Current value, loan balance or payoff quote, capital repairs due in the next three years, selling costs from an agent net sheet, and net proceeds. Add trailing-12 NOI, annual debt service, personal-use days for each of the last two years, depreciation taken to date by asset class, and any suspended passive losses. The last two come from your tax returns.

This slide is Part B. One column per option. Cash now, the tax estimate your CPA gives you, cash after tax, debt, cash flow in a base and weak case, how long it takes, and how many hours a month it costs you afterward.

Then return on after-tax equity: cash flow divided by cash after tax. And one more row on the full worksheet: what the cash would do instead. That's your opportunity cost, written down.

End with one decision, a one-sentence reason, a recheck date, and who approved it.

slides.title: If you choose the exchange, clear this checklist before the sale closes
items: Relinquished property held for business or investment (CPA)
Personal use fits Rev. Proc. 2008-16 or other support (CPA)
QI chosen, not a disqualified agent, funds holding known
Sale closing date (title or escrow)
Day 45 written identification date (QI)
Day 180 or return due date, whichever is earlier (CPA)
Replacements identified, each with an SR.1 check
Replacement price and loan planned; effect of cash or a smaller loan (CPA, lender)
Furniture handled outside the exchange (CPA)
Everyone who must approve: owners, lender, partners
slides.notes:
Part C is the 1031 checklist. You only fill it in if the exchange is your choice.

Each line has someone who confirms it. Your CPA confirms the property is held for investment, whether your personal use fits Rev. Proc. 2008-16, and the real deadline. Your attorney and CPA help you vet the QI. Title or escrow gives you the closing date. The QI tracks day 45.

Then the replacement side. Every property you identify needs an address-level permission check with SR.1, confirmed by the licensing office or an attorney. You need a planned price and loan. Ask your CPA and lender what happens if you take cash out or end up with a smaller loan than before.

The furniture goes outside the exchange, so the CPA handles it separately.

And last, list who must approve. All owners, the lender, and any partners. Line up those approvals before the clock starts.

slides.title: An exit is only as good as four records you keep from day one
slides.text: Every input traces back to the track: goals (PA.1), the weak-case test (0.3, PA.6, PA.7), depreciation (PA.10, Sam's PA.5, SR.3), repairs (PA.9, OP.8), and the trailing 12 (OP.10, OP.11).
items: Closing documents
Every depreciation schedule your CPA files
Receipts for improvements and repairs
A calendar of rental and personal-use days
slides.notes:
This is the last lesson in STR Concierge, so look at where the worksheet's inputs came from.

The goals in your exit decision are the goals from your PA.1 buy box. The weak-case test is the same one you ran in 0.3, PA.6, and PA.7. The depreciation history comes from the choices you made with your CPA in PA.10 and Sam's PA.5, using SR.3. The capital repair list comes from your PA.9 inspection and your OP.8 maintenance records. The trailing 12 comes from the review habit Sam set up in OP.10 and that you extended in OP.11.

So keep four things from day one. Closing documents. Every depreciation schedule your CPA files. Receipts for improvements and repairs. And a calendar of rental and personal-use days.

With those, any of the four options is a short conversation. Without them, even a good sale turns into a reconstruction project.

slides.title: A broker, servicer, CPA, QI, lender, and licensing office each confirm one piece
rows: Current market value; whether furniture or future bookings add anything a buyer will pay for
A written payoff quote and any prepayment penalty
Adjusted basis, depreciation by asset, allocation to section 1245 items, the gain split, rates, state tax, suspended losses, other federal taxes
Held for investment; personal use and Rev. Proc. 2008-16; how cash or debt changes are reported on Form 8824
QI, and an attorney if needed
The exchange agreement, how funds are held, the day-45 and day-180 dates
In writing: value, LTV, rate, costs, and reserves
Any replacement property's exact address permits your planned use
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what.

A broker or appraiser confirms value, and whether furniture or future bookings add anything a buyer will actually pay for. Your loan servicer gives you a written payoff quote and tells you about any prepayment penalty.

Your CPA carries the most weight here. On a sale, they confirm the adjusted basis, depreciation allowed or allowable by asset, and the allocation of price to section 1245 items. They also confirm the gain split, the rates, state tax, any suspended passive losses, and any other federal taxes. On an exchange, they confirm investment use, whether your personal use fits Rev. Proc. 2008-16, and how cash or debt changes show up on Form 8824.

The QI, with an attorney if you need one, confirms the exchange agreement, how funds are held, and the two dates. The refinance lender confirms terms in writing. And the licensing office or an STR attorney checks any replacement's exact address.

slides.title: Four requests this week give you real numbers for every column
items: Ask a broker for an opinion of value and your agent for a line-by-line seller net sheet.
Request a written payoff quote from your loan servicer.
Pull depreciation taken to date, by asset class, from your filed tax returns.
Count your personal-use days for each of the last 2 years from your calendar.
slides.next: This closes STR Concierge. Holding: rerun this yearly after Sam's OP.10 reviews. Buying again: start at **PA.1 Discovery: Defining Your Buy Box**. Tax side: fill in **SR.3** before you meet your CPA.
slides.notes:
Four things to do this week. Ask a broker for an opinion of value, and ask your agent for a line-by-line seller net sheet. Request a written payoff quote from your servicer. Pull the depreciation you've taken to date, by asset class, from your filed returns. And count your personal-use days for each of the last two years.

That closes STR Concierge.

If your decision is to hold, go back to Sam's OP.10 review each quarter, and rerun this worksheet at least once a year.

If you're buying again, whether by exchange or with sale proceeds, start at PA.1, Discovery: Defining Your Buy Box, with updated goals. The course path starts over from there: market and deal review, financing, diligence, closing, launch, and the 30- and 90-day review.

For the tax side, open resource SR.3 and fill in your actual depreciation history before you meet your CPA.

slides.title: Every tax and exchange rule here traces to an IRS publication or notice

items.title: IRS Publication 544, Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets
items.note: Adjusted basis; allowed or allowable; section 1245 ordinary gain; section 1231 gain

items.title: IRS Publication 527, Residential Rental Property
items.note: Basis reduced by depreciation you could have deducted, bonus, and section 179

items.title: IRS Topic 409, Capital gains and losses
items.note: Unrecaptured section 1250 gain taxed at a maximum 25%

items.title: IRS Publication 925
items.note: Passive activity rules; the suspended-loss question for your CPA

items.title: IRS: Like-kind exchanges, real estate tax tips
items.note: Real property only; investment use; 45 and 180 days; QI and disqualified agents

items.title: IRS Rev. Proc. 2008-16
items.note: Safe harbor for dwelling units with occasional personal use; section 4.02 standards

slides.notes:
These are the sources behind this lesson.

Publication 544 covers adjusted basis, the allowed-or-allowable rule, section 1245 gain as ordinary income, and section 1231 gain. Publication 527 covers how depreciation, bonus, and section 179 reduce basis. Topic 409 gives the 25% maximum rate on unrecaptured section 1250 gain. Publication 925 covers passive activity rules. How a sale affects suspended losses is a question I've left for your CPA.

For exchanges, the IRS real estate tips page covers what qualifies, the two deadlines, and who can't be your QI. The Form 8824 instructions cover reporting and timing. Rev. Proc. 2008-16 is the safe harbor for units with some personal use. Confirm its exact day and month standards with your CPA against the IRS text.

The Cedar Ridge figures come from cases B4, B6, B7, and B8. The year-5 refinance, the gain split, the allocations, and the placeholder rates are new assumptions for teaching.
